title: Expanding the Volatile Abundance Inventory for High-Priority K-Dwarf JWST Exoplanet Systems
comment: 32 pages, 6 figures, 5 tables. Accepted for publication in ApJ (11/3/2026)
summary: There are exceedingly few chemical abundance measurements available in the literature for K dwarf stars, especially for those with T$_{eff} <$ 4700 K due to an incompatibility of traditional analyses with their molecular-line-ridden optical spectra. To address the need for K dwarf abundance constraints, we present an elemental ([C/H], [O/H]) and isotopic ($^{12}$C/$^{13}$C, $^{16}$O/$^{18}$O) abundance analysis for six K dwarf exoplanet host stars: K2-141, NGTS-10, WASP-43, WASP-69, WASP-80, and HATS-72. Each system hosts an exoplanet targeted by JWST characterization efforts, making host star abundances especially critical as baseline references. Using MARCS model atmospheres, the TurboSpectrum spectral synthesis code, and near-infrared IGRINS spectra, we derive novel [C/H] and [O/H] abundance ratios for these high-priority K dwarf host stars. We further investigate prospects for determining $^{12}$C/$^{13}$C and $^{16}$O/$^{18}$O ratios using $^{13}$C$^{16}$O and $^{12}$C$^{18}$O lines from the 2.3 micron CO bandhead. The observed spectra are too noisy to measure $^{16}$O/$^{18}$O ratios for the sample, but we do find sub-solar $^{12}$C/$^{13}$C ratios for five out of six targets. We also derive uniform gyrochronological ages for each host star to compare with galactic chemical evolution models and identify underlying abundance-age trends. NIR H+K band spectroscopy provides an alternative to optical, atomic line-derived carbon and oxygen abundances for cool dwarf stars. The growing catalog of precise host star elemental and isotopic abundances complements ongoing observations of their companions and provides a baseline for understanding their chemical composition, origin, and evolution.

AI.tldr: This paper measures carbon and oxygen elemental abundances and carbon/oxygen isotopic ratios for six cool K dwarf exoplanet host stars using near-infrared IGRINS spectra and spectral synthesis, addressing the scarcity of abundance data for K dwarfs with T_eff < 4700 K.
AI.motivation: Chemical abundance measurements for K dwarfs—especially those cooler than 4700 K—are extremely scarce because their optical spectra are heavily contaminated by molecular lines, which defeats traditional analysis methods. Since these stars host exoplanets being characterized by JWST, accurate host-star abundances are needed as baseline references for interpreting planetary compositions and formation histories.
AI.method: The authors performed an elemental ([C/H], [O/H]) and isotopic (12C/13C, 16O/18O) abundance analysis on six K dwarf exoplanet hosts (K2-141, NGTS-10, WASP-43, WASP-69, WASP-80, HATS-72). They used MARCS model atmospheres, the TurboSpectrum spectral synthesis code, and near-infrared IGRINS spectra, targeting 13C16O and 12C18O lines in the 2.3 micron CO bandhead. They also derived uniform gyrochronological ages to compare with galactic chemical evolution models and probe abundance-age trends.
AI.result: New [C/H] and [O/H] abundance ratios were derived for all six high-priority K dwarf hosts. The spectra were too noisy to measure 16O/18O ratios, but sub-solar 12C/13C ratios were found for five of the six targets. Uniform gyrochronological ages enabled comparison with galactic chemical evolution models and identification of abundance-age trends.
AI.conclusion: Near-infrared H+K band spectroscopy offers a viable alternative to optical atomic line analyses for deriving carbon and oxygen abundances in cool dwarf stars. The growing catalog of precise elemental and isotopic host-star abundances complements companion observations and provides a baseline for understanding stellar chemical composition, origin, and evolution.

title: Constraining the Merger Fraction and the Upper Mass Limit of Ultramassive White Dwarfs
summary: We performed a spectroscopic survey of all known white dwarfs with $M \geq 1.3~M_\odot$ and $T_{\rm eff}\geq11,000$ K identified through Gaia DR3 astrometry from the Gentile-Fusillo et al. (2021) catalog. Of the 293 white dwarf candidates that met our criteria, 259 had no optical spectroscopy or spectral classification available in the literature. We obtained follow-up spectroscopy on 97% of this sample and performed a detailed model atmosphere analysis to constrain the atmospheric composition and mass for each object. For a selection of magnetic white dwarfs, we use offset dipole models to constrain the magnetic field strength and geometry and calculate the magnetic fraction as a function of mass. We use magnetism, unusual atmospheric composition, kinematics, and rapid rotation rates to identify merger remnants, and constrain the merger fraction to be $53_{-6}^{+7}$% for white dwarfs more massive than $1.3~M_\odot$. Hence, roughly half of the most massive white dwarfs likely form through binary mergers. We also use our sample to derive an empirical upper mass limit for white dwarfs in the solar neighborhood. Including the General Relativistic effects, the most massive white dwarf in our sample, J0318+7923, has $M=1.33-1.35~M_\odot$ depending on the unknown core composition. Furthermore, because our temperature criteria overlap with the ZZ Ceti instability strip, we find a new selection of ultramassive pulsator candidates that may provide an excellent opportunity to probe the interiors of crystallized CO or ONe-core white dwarfs.

AI.tldr: A spectroscopic survey of 293 massive (M ≥ 1.3 M☉) white dwarfs from Gaia DR3 finds that ~53% are merger remnants, derives an empirical upper mass limit of ~1.33–1.35 M☉, and identifies new ultramassive pulsator candidates.
AI.motivation: Massive white dwarfs probe stellar evolution endpoints, merger channels, and the empirical upper mass limit, yet the majority of high-mass candidates lacked optical spectroscopy or spectral classification, leaving their nature (merger remnants vs. single-star remnants) and mass distribution poorly constrained.
AI.method: Selected all known white dwarfs with M ≥ 1.3 M☉ and T_eff ≥ 11,000 K from the Gentile-Fusillo et al. (2021) Gaia DR3 catalog (293 candidates; 259 previously unclassified). Obtained follow-up optical spectroscopy for 97% of the sample, then performed detailed model atmosphere analysis to constrain atmospheric composition and mass. For magnetic white dwarfs, offset dipole models constrained field strength and geometry, and the magnetic fraction was computed as a function of mass. Magnetism, peculiar atmospheric composition, kinematics, and rapid rotation were used as merger-remnant diagnostics.
AI.result: The merger fraction for white dwarfs above 1.3 M☉ is 53(-6)(+7)%, implying roughly half of the most massive white dwarfs form via binary mergers. Including general relativistic effects, the most massive object in the sample, J0318+7923, has M = 1.33–1.35 M☉ depending on the unknown core composition, defining an empirical upper mass limit for solar-neighborhood white dwarfs. Overlap of the temperature criterion with the ZZ Ceti instability strip yields a new selection of ultramassive pulsator candidates.
AI.conclusion: Binary mergers are the dominant formation channel for the most massive white dwarfs, and the empirically derived upper mass limit (~1.33–1.35 M☉) is consistent with general relativistic stability constraints. The newly identified ultramassive pulsator candidates offer a promising opportunity to probe the interiors of crystallized CO- and ONe-core white dwarfs via asteroseismology.

title: The Complex Magnetic Anatomy of a White Dwarf Chromosphere
comment: 11 pages, 5 figures, 2 tables, accepted to MNRAS
summary: This study presents phase-resolved spectroscopy and spectropolarimetry of the DAHe white dwarf LP 705-64. Here, two apparently discrete chromospheric regions are observed to alternate in visibility and magnetic polarity with rotation, with field strengths of 9.5 and 22 MG based on the measured Zeeman splitting in Hα. As in the class prototype GD 356, emission line equivalent widths vary in antiphase with the broadband light curve. The 9.5 MG field is visible for 60 per cent of the stellar rotation and stays nearly constant, whereas the 22 MG field increases modestly during the remaining phases. Notably, the time-series transitions between magnetic regions are abrupt and transit-like in morphology, requiring at least one magnetic region to be highly localised and significantly smaller than the areas inferred for the dark surface spots. Both the intensity and the Stokes V/I spectra indicate a field configuration significantly more complex than an offset dipole, but higher-cadence data are necessary to distinguish between a global field and localised magnetic regions. All data are consistent with magnetic, chromospheric, and dark surface regions that are co-located and thus physically related. These findings support a model of chromospheric emission that is intrinsic and localised, consistent with predictions of dynamo-driven electrical currents that heat the upper atmosphere near magnetic poles.

AI.tldr: Phase-resolved spectroscopy and spectropolarimetry of the DAHe white dwarf LP 705-64 reveal two discrete chromospheric regions that alternate with rotation, showing 9.5 MG and 22 MG fields, abrupt transit-like transitions, and emission variability consistent with localized dynamo-driven heating co-located with magnetic and dark surface regions.
AI.motivation: Motivated by the class prototype GD 356, the study aims to characterize the magnetic and chromospheric structure of LP 705-64, testing whether chromospheric emission is intrinsic and localized and how it relates to magnetic fields and dark surface spots.
AI.method: Phase-resolved spectroscopy and spectropolarimetry (intensity and Stokes V/I spectra), measuring Zeeman splitting of Hα to infer field strengths, and comparing emission-line equivalent widths with the broadband light curve.
AI.result: Two apparently discrete chromospheric regions alternate in visibility and magnetic polarity with rotation, with field strengths of 9.5 MG (visible ~60% of the rotation, nearly constant) and 22 MG (increasing modestly during remaining phases). Emission equivalent widths vary in antiphase with the broadband light curve, as in GD 356. Transitions between regions are abrupt and transit-like, requiring at least one highly localized, small magnetic region. The field configuration is significantly more complex than an offset dipole.
AI.conclusion: The data are consistent with co-located magnetic, chromospheric, and dark surface regions that are physically related, supporting intrinsic localized chromospheric emission consistent with dynamo-driven electrical currents heating the upper atmosphere near magnetic poles; higher-cadence data are needed to distinguish a global field from localized magnetic regions.

title: Interferometric survey of stellar parameters. Reliable methodology for a direct measurement of the angular diameter in exoplanet host stars
summary: Since their pioneer observations more than thirty years ago, exoplanets have been a major topic among the astrophysics community. Despite their ubiquity, our knowledge of planetary parameters and internal compositions still mostly relies on stellar quantities estimated through evolutionary models, which suffer from a calibration bias, preventing the community to have accurate discussions on the diversity of planets across the Universe. We use our sample to demonstrate the current best reachable precision of the CHARA Array to be $\sim$ 2% on radius determination, with an error budget dominated by the uncertainty on the angular diameter, while systematics are shown to be of the order of 1% thanks to our methodology. While the precision matches values found in the literature, we demonstrate the uniqueness of the present study in the relevance of the results put forward. Finally, we show that our methods naturally translate into an improved accuracy of the planetary parameters, along with an improvement in precision by $\sim$ 50% in radius and $\sim$ 30% in mass.

AI.tldr: Using interferometric observations from the CHARA Array, the authors determine exoplanet host star radii to ~2% precision with ~1% systematics, and show this improves planetary radius and mass estimates.
AI.motivation: Exoplanet parameters and internal compositions mostly rely on stellar quantities derived from evolutionary models, which carry calibration biases that limit accurate comparison of planetary diversity.
AI.method: Interferometric radius measurements of host stars with the CHARA Array, combined with a methodology designed to control systematic errors, applied to a sample of exoplanet hosts.
AI.result: Achieves ~2% precision on stellar radius, dominated by angular diameter uncertainty, with systematics around 1%. Translating this into planetary parameters yields improved accuracy and ~50% better precision in radius and ~30% in mass.
AI.conclusion: Direct interferometric stellar radii bypass evolutionary-model calibration bias, providing more accurate planetary parameters and demonstrating the value of the approach despite precision matching literature values.

title: Tidal Braking Does Not Dominate Open-Cluster Slow Rotators
summary: Extended main-sequence turn-offs (eMSTOs) observed in open clusters younger than $2~\mathrm{Gyr}$ are commonly attributed to a spread in stellar rotation rates. Tidal synchronization in close binary systems has been proposed as a possible mechanism for producing slowly rotating stars. To test this hypothesis, we measured the radial-velocity (RV) dispersions of slow-rotator samples associated with the eMSTOs of eight open clusters using ESO VLT/GIRAFFE and SALT/RSS spectroscopy. We extended the analysis to 40 open clusters using Gaia DR3 RV measurements. The observed cluster RV dispersions are generally substantially smaller than those predicted for binary populations dominated by close systems with orbital periods for which tidal synchronization is expected to be effective. In particular, all 40 clusters in the Gaia sample have RV dispersions below the prediction of the $P=10$ d binary-population model. These results suggest that close, tidally synchronized binaries are unlikely to be the dominant origin of slow-rotator populations in young and intermediate-age open clusters, although a contribution from undetected or wider binary systems cannot be excluded.

AI.tldr: Tidal synchronization in close binaries is unlikely to dominate the slow-rotator populations linked to extended main-sequence turn-offs in young open clusters, as observed RV dispersions fall below model predictions.
AI.motivation: Extended main-sequence turn-offs (eMSTOs) in open clusters younger than 2 Gyr are widely attributed to a spread in stellar rotation rates. Because slow rotators must be explained, tidal synchronization in close binary systems has been proposed as a mechanism to spin down stars and thus produce the slow-rotator population. This paper tests whether close, tidally synchronized binaries are the dominant source of these slow rotators.
AI.method: The authors measured radial-velocity (RV) dispersions of slow-rotator samples associated with the eMSTOs of eight open clusters using ESO VLT/GIRAFFE and SALT/RSS spectroscopy, then extended the analysis to 40 open clusters using Gaia DR3 RV measurements. They compared the observed cluster RV dispersions with predictions from binary-population models dominated by close systems at orbital periods where tidal synchronization is expected to be effective (e.g., P = 10 d).
AI.result: Observed cluster RV dispersions are generally substantially smaller than predicted for binary populations dominated by close systems subject to effective tidal synchronization. In particular, all 40 clusters in the Gaia sample show RV dispersions below the prediction of the P = 10 d binary-population model.
AI.conclusion: Close, tidally synchronized binaries are unlikely to be the dominant origin of slow-rotator populations in young and intermediate-age open clusters, though a contribution from undetected or wider binary systems cannot be excluded.

title: Dynamical formation of Gaia neutron star binaries in star clusters as a phase-dependent process
comment: 14 pages, 6 figures, 1 table. Accepted for publication in ApJ
summary: Gaia has discovered dormant compact-object binaries in which the compact object shows no observable interaction with its luminous companion. These systems, hereafter Gaia BHs and Gaia NSs for black hole (BH) and neutron star (NS) companions, provide a new probe of compact-object binary formation. These detached systems are difficult to produce through standard isolated binary evolution alone, and their formation pathways remain unclear. Previous $N$-body studies have shown that Gaia BH-like objects are formed efficiently in star clusters, while Gaia NS-like objects are not. This has been attributed to the BH subsystem dominating the cluster core. We performed direct $N$-body simulations of $10^4 \mathrm{M}_\odot$ star clusters in a Galactic tidal field and investigated how NS-main-sequence (NS-MS) binaries form during the late BH-depleted phase. We found that NS-MS binaries satisfying Gaia-sensitive criteria form only after BH depletion. NSs are present in the core throughout the evolution, but the strong encounters there are monopolized by the BH subsystem until it is depleted. Our results show that the dynamical formation of Gaia-sensitive NS-MS systems is not prevented in star clusters, but delayed relative to Gaia BH-like systems.

AI.tldr: Direct N-body simulations of 10^4 M_sun clusters in a Galactic tidal field show that Gaia-sensitive NS-MS binaries form only after the BH subsystem is depleted, indicating their dynamical formation is delayed, not suppressed.
AI.motivation: Gaia-discovered dormant compact-object binaries (Gaia BHs, Gaia NSs) are hard to form via isolated binary evolution, and prior N-body work found clusters efficiently make Gaia BH-like objects but not Gaia NS-like ones—an asymmetry attributed to BH-subsystem dominance of the core.
AI.method: Direct N-body simulations of 10^4 M_sun star clusters in a Galactic tidal field, tracking NS-main-sequence binary formation across evolutionary phases, especially the late BH-depleted phase.
AI.result: NS-MS binaries meeting Gaia-sensitive criteria form only after BH depletion; NSs are present in the core throughout, but strong encounters are monopolized by the BH subsystem until it is depleted.
AI.conclusion: Dynamical formation of Gaia-sensitive NS-MS systems is not prevented in star clusters but is delayed relative to Gaia BH-like systems; cluster formation channels for Gaia NSs remain viable at late times.

title: Chromospherically Active Stars in the MeerKAT Galactic Plane Survey
comment: 13 pages, 8 figures, 1 table. Published in MNRAS (https://academic.oup.com/mnras/article/553/1/stag1821/8834026). Part of the online supplemental information is included
summary: Stellar magnetic activity has long been established to occur in subsets of late-type main-sequence stars and manifests itself in the form of chromospheric and coronal activity. This activity is driven by magnetic fields generated by dynamo mechanisms associated with stellar rotation and convection, which channel and dissipate magnetic energy to the outer atmospheric layers. Optical spectroscopic follow-up was carried out for 99 radio-X-ray coronally active stars of G-, K-, and M-spectral types in the SARAO MeerKAT Galactic plane survey point sources. There are 46 stars that exhibited chromospheric activity. Specifically, 39 stars show Ca II H&K emission lines, whereas 18 show Ca II IRT, 11 show both H&K and IRT lines. Of the 39 stars displaying H&K emission, 37 show activity levels greater than the Solar minimum activity. Their X-ray to bolometric luminosity ratios are within the coronal thresholds of > -4.5. In addition, we explored optical photometry to investigate the rotation information and found that these stars show short rotation periods; in comparison with activity levels, the activity levels dampen as the rotation periods increase. We also analysed optical light curves for a subset of stars, and they show flaring behaviour at the same epoch as enhanced chromospheric activity, indicating the flares and chromospheric emission are manifestations of the same underlying magnetic activity process.

AI.tldr: Optical spectroscopy of 99 radio-X-ray coronally active G/K/M stars from the MeerKAT Galactic plane survey finds 46 chromospherically active stars, with activity signatures linked to short rotation periods and contemporaneous flaring.
AI.motivation: Stellar magnetic activity in late-type main-sequence stars, driven by rotation- and convection-based dynamo mechanisms, manifests as chromospheric and coronal emission. The study aims to characterize the optical chromospheric activity of a sample of radio-X-ray coronally active stars and relate it to rotation and flaring.
AI.method: Optical spectroscopic follow-up of 99 radio-X-ray coronally active G-, K-, and M-type stars identified as point sources in the SARAO MeerKAT Galactic plane survey, examining Ca II H&K and Ca II IRT emission, X-ray-to-bolometric luminosity ratios, optical photometry for rotation periods, and optical light curves for flaring.
AI.result: 46 stars show chromospheric activity: 39 with Ca II H&K emission, 18 with Ca II IRT, and 11 with both. Of the 39 H&K emitters, 37 exceed Solar-minimum activity levels, and their X-ray-to-bolometric luminosity ratios fall within the coronal threshold (> -4.5). Stars show short rotation periods, with activity levels damping as rotation periods increase. A subset exhibits flaring at the same epoch as enhanced chromospheric activity.
AI.conclusion: Chromospheric activity, coronal X-ray emission, rapid rotation, and flaring are co-manifestations of the same underlying magnetic activity process in these late-type stars, consistent with rotation-convection dynamo-driven activity.

title: Successive Decimetric Bursts Associated with Breakout Magnetic Reconnection during the Decay Phase of an M-Class Flare
summary: Radio imaging spectroscopy diagnoses coronal electron acceleration and propagation by tracking energetic electron beams and locating energy-release sites. Using MUSER (0.4-2 GHz) and SDO data, we investigate decimetric radio emission during an eruption with an M1.1 flare on 17 December 2014. The eruption involves a twisted coronal structure evolving through three stages: a violent internal eruption, a rise-and-expansion phase, and a breakout eruption. The flare peaks at 01:50 UT during the internal eruption, while the cluster of successive type III-like decimetric bursts occurs in the decay phase, linked to the breakout eruption. The radio source coincides with a high-squashing-factor Q region from nonlinear force-free field (NLFFF) extrapolations, indicating a quasi-separatrix layer (QSL). We interpret the radio emission as consistent with plasma emission driven by nonthermal electrons accelerated by breakout reconnection at this QSL, between the outer envelope of the erupting structure and the surrounding corona. The successive bursts occur in the decay phase because breakout reconnection involves a larger, more energetic twisted structure at higher altitude, where an extended high-Q region, favorable acceleration geometry, and repeated sub-eruptions sustain efficient electron acceleration. Missing soft X-ray enhancement suggests most accelerated electrons escape upward or lose energy before reaching the chromosphere. The concentrated source positions of the successive radio bursts suggest pseudostreamers may act as particle accelerators, trapping electrons and directing them along a narrow layer. These results establish decimetric radio imaging as a powerful diagnostic of breakout reconnection and particle acceleration in the solar corona, with implications for energy release in pseudostreamer environments.

AI.tldr: Using MUSER (0.4–2 GHz) and SDO data, the paper shows that successive type III-like decimetric bursts in the decay phase of a 17 Dec 2014 M1.1 eruptive flare are plasma emission from nonthermal electrons accelerated by breakout reconnection at a quasi-separatrix layer coincident with a high-squashing-factor region, suggesting pseudostreamers can act as particle accelerators.
AI.motivation: Radio imaging spectroscopy is a key tool for diagnosing coronal electron acceleration and propagation, yet the link between specific reconnection geometries (e.g., breakout reconnection, QSLs) and the observed decimetric burst emission—especially bursts occurring in the flare decay phase rather than at flare peak—remains poorly constrained. The authors aim to identify the acceleration site and mechanism responsible for successive decimetric bursts during an eruptive event.
AI.method: Multi-wavelength analysis of the 17 December 2014 M1.1 eruptive flare using MUSER (0.4–2 GHz) radio imaging spectroscopy combined with SDO observations. The eruption's twisted coronal structure is tracked through three stages (internal eruption, rise-and-expansion, breakout eruption). Radio source positions are compared with nonlinear force-free field (NLFFF) extrapolations to compute the squashing factor Q and locate quasi-separatrix layers (QSLs).
AI.result: The flare peaks at 01:50 UT during the internal eruption, whereas the cluster of successive type III-like decimetric bursts occurs in the decay phase and is linked to the breakout eruption. The radio source coincides with a high-Q region (QSL) between the outer envelope of the erupting structure and the surrounding corona. The emission is consistent with plasma emission driven by nonthermal electrons accelerated by breakout reconnection at this QSL. Bursts occur in the decay phase because breakout reconnection involves a larger, more energetic twisted structure at higher altitude, where an extended high-Q region, favorable acceleration geometry, and repeated sub-eruptions sustain efficient acceleration. No soft X-ray enhancement is observed, implying most accelerated electrons escape upward or lose energy before reaching the chromosphere. The concentrated source positions suggest pseudostreamers act as particle accelerators, trapping electrons and guiding them along a narrow layer.
AI.conclusion: Decimetric radio imaging is established as a powerful diagnostic of breakout reconnection and particle acceleration in the solar corona, with implications for energy release in pseudostreamer environments. The results support a scenario in which breakout reconnection at a high-Q QSL drives sustained electron acceleration, with pseudostreamers potentially functioning as efficient particle accelerators.

title: Existence of Distinct Strong and Weak Shear Regimes of Self-Generated Turbulent Magnetic Reconnection
comment: 7 pages, 3 figures, accepted for the Astrophysical Journal Letters
summary: Magnetic reconnection can become fast in three-dimensional turbulent layers. However, the parameters and mechanisms that control the fast state are not yet fully clear. Existing guide-field simulations of self-generated turbulent reconnection show locally coherent flux-rope structures embedded in a stochastic layer, motivating a flux-rope-mediated picture, with reconnection rates of order $V_{\rm rec}/V_A \sim 0.01$ in MHD. Here, we test whether and how magnetic shear changes the reconnection regime, using 3D resistive-MHD simulations at $S_L=10^5$. We vary the guide field while keeping the initial reconnecting field strength and rate normalization fixed, comparing a guide-field, weaker-shear configuration with the anti-parallel, strong-shear limit. We find that the strong-shear regime is qualitatively distinct from the flux-rope-mediated guide-field regime. Rather than retaining a narrow layer and locally coherent flux-rope structures, the current layer develops short-wavelength corrugations that broaden it substantially, and the reconnection layer electric field is sustained by fluctuation EMF. The reconnection rate increases to $V_{\rm rec}/V_A \sim 0.03$, about three times the guide-field value. These results indicate that magnetic shear can select the mechanism controlling fast 3D turbulent reconnection, shifting the system from a guide-field regime consistent with flux-rope mediation toward a very fast turbulence-broadened regime. This transition provides a novel explanation for the sudden switch-on of fast reconnection in eruptive solar flares.

AI.tldr: Using 3D resistive-MHD simulations at \(S_L=10^5\), the authors show that magnetic shear selects the mechanism of fast turbulent reconnection: strong shear produces a turbulence-broadened layer with fluctuation-EMF-driven electric field and rates \(V_{\rm rec}/V_A\sim0.03\), about three times the flux-rope-mediated guide-field regime, offering an explanation for the sudden onset of fast reconnection in eruptive solar flares.
AI.motivation: Fast reconnection in 3D turbulent layers is observed, but the parameters and mechanisms controlling the fast state remain unclear. Prior guide-field simulations of self-generated turbulent reconnection reveal locally coherent flux-rope structures in a stochastic layer (flux-rope-mediated picture, rates ~0.01 in MHD). The paper tests whether and how magnetic shear changes the reconnection regime.
AI.method: 3D resistive-MHD simulations at Lundquist number \(S_L=10^5\). The guide field is varied while initial reconnecting field strength and rate normalization are held fixed, comparing a guide-field, weaker-shear configuration against the anti-parallel, strong-shear limit.
AI.result: The strong-shear regime is qualitatively distinct from the flux-rope-mediated guide-field regime. Instead of a narrow layer with locally coherent flux-rope structures, the current layer develops short-wavelength corrugations that substantially broaden it, and the reconnection-layer electric field is sustained by fluctuation EMF. The reconnection rate rises to \(V_{\rm rec}/V_A\sim0.03\), roughly three times the guide-field value.
AI.conclusion: Magnetic shear can select the mechanism controlling fast 3D turbulent reconnection, shifting the system from a flux-rope-mediated guide-field regime toward a very fast, turbulence-broadened regime. This transition provides a novel explanation for the sudden switch-on of fast reconnection in eruptive solar flares.

title: The OpenMULTI3D stellar analysis package. A 3D non-LTE spectrum synthesis code for AFGKM-type stars within the DISPATCH framework
comment: Accepted for publication in A&A. 22 pages, 12 figures, 9 tables. Code available at https://github.com/Bergemann-Group-development/dispatch
summary: Upcoming large spectroscopic surveys such as WEAVE, 4MOST, and SDSS-V will provide millions of high-resolution stellar spectra. This motivates the development of efficient codes to perform three-dimensional (3D) non-local thermodynamic equilibrium (non-LTE) radiative transfer (RT) calculations, in order to meet the requirements on efficiency and data analysis quality set by these surveys. We present a new open access 3D non-LTE spectrum synthesis code OpenMULTI3D, based on its predecessor MULTI3D, which was never released. This code can be used to compute large grids of spectra of AFGKM-type stars and will aid the exploitation of large-scale spectroscopic surveys such as 4MOST. We summarise the main input micro- and macro-physics of the code, describe its numerical implementation and provide selected test cases. The outputs of the code are compared with standard results in the literature, including the NLTE departure coefficients in 1D and 3D, the 3D NLTE abundance corrections, 3D synthetic spectral energy distributions for three types of stars, and 3D NLTE Balmer-line profiles of a metal-poor red giant. We also demonstrate how the code can be used to compute time-dependent spectra of stars, which may be relevant in precision stellar physics and analyses of exoplanet spectra. OpenMULTI3D offers an accessible and efficient platform for high-fidelity stellar analysis in the era of large-scale spectroscopic surveys.

AI.tldr: OpenMULTI3D is a new open-access 3D non-LTE radiative transfer code, derived from the unreleased MULTI3D, that synthesizes large grids of spectra for AFGKM stars at 4MOST, WEAVE and SDSS-V, validated against literature benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Upcoming large spectroscopic surveys (WEAVE, 4MOST, SDSS-V) will deliver millions of high-resolution stellar spectra, creating a need for efficient, accurate 3D non-LTE radiative transfer codes to keep pace with the data volume and analysis-quality requirements.
AI.method: The authors present OpenMULTI3D, a successor to the never-released MULTI3D, and describe its input micro- and macro-physics, numerical implementation, and validation test cases against standard literature results.
AI.result: Agreement with literature is demonstrated for 1D and 3D NLTE departure coefficients, 3D NLTE abundance corrections, 3D synthetic spectral energy distributions of three stellar types, and 3D NLTE Balmer-line profiles of a metal-poor red giant; the code additionally supports time-dependent spectra.
AI.conclusion: OpenMULTI3D provides an accessible, efficient platform for high-fidelity 3D non-LTE stellar analysis, supporting large-scale surveys such as 4MOST and precision applications including exoplanet spectral analyses.

title: A joint astrometric, eclipse timing and radial velocity orbit for the hierarchical triple V819 Herculis
comment: Accepted for publication in MNRAS. 14 pages, 7 figures, 6 tables
summary: We present a joint Bayesian orbital analysis of the hierarchical triple system V819 Herculis using ground-based astrometry, radial velocities (RV), and eclipse timing variations (ETV). By coupling these complementary data sets within a physically consistent Keplerian framework, we obtain a self-consistent three-dimensional solution for the outer orbit and the dynamical properties of the system. The outer orbit is found to have a period of $P_3 = 2016.97 \pm 0.27$ d and a high eccentricity of $e_3 = 0.6800 \pm 0.0016$, with the same orbital geometry simultaneously reproducing the sky-plane astrometry, the LiTE signal in the eclipse timings, and the tertiary radial velocities. The joint solution determines the component masses dynamically from these data alone, yielding $M_{12} = 2.721 \pm 0.055\,M_\odot$ for the inner binary and $M_3 = 1.954 \pm 0.070\,M_\odot$ for the tertiary, together with a LiTE amplitude of $A_\mathrm{LiTE} = 0.0104$ d and an RV semi-amplitude of $K_3 = 18.46$ km s$^{-1}$. The joint fit also yields an orbital parallax of $π_\mathrm{orb} = 14.08 \pm 0.13$ mas, consistent with Gaia DR3, Gaia DR2 and the HIPPARCOS New Reduction. The derived tertiary mass is higher than expected for a standard G8-type main-sequence star, suggesting that the tertiary component may be in an advanced evolutionary stage. The resulting outer orbit is well constrained, and the system is strongly hierarchical, with an outer period about 900 times the inner one. Finally, we provide predicted astrometric positions for the tertiary component for five years beyond 2026.5 to guide future high-precision observations.

AI.tldr: A joint Bayesian fit of astrometry, radial velocities and eclipse timing variations yields a self-consistent 3D orbit and dynamical masses for the hierarchical triple V819 Herculis.
AI.motivation: The system's outer orbit and dynamical properties require combining complementary, individually incomplete datasets; a physically consistent Keplerian framework can simultaneously reproduce sky-plane astrometry, the light-time effect (LiTE) in eclipse timings, and tertiary radial velocities, thereby breaking degeneracies and delivering model-independent masses.
AI.method: Joint Bayesian orbital analysis coupling ground-based astrometry, radial velocities (RV) and eclipse timing variations (ETV) within a single self-consistent Keplerian model of the hierarchical triple, fitting the outer orbit geometry and the inner binary simultaneously.
AI.result: Outer period P3 = 2016.97 ± 0.27 d, high eccentricity e3 = 0.6800 ± 0.0016; dynamical masses M12 = 2.721 ± 0.055 M_sun and M3 = 1.954 ± 0.070 M_sun; LiTE amplitude A_LiTE = 0.0104 d and RV semi-amplitude K3 = 18.46 km/s; orbital parallax π_orb = 14.08 ± 0.13 mas, consistent with Gaia DR3, Gaia DR2 and the HIPPARCOS New Reduction. The tertiary mass exceeds expectations for a standard G8 main-sequence star, hinting at an advanced evolutionary stage.
AI.conclusion: The outer orbit is well constrained and the system is strongly hierarchical (outer period ~900 times the inner). Dynamical masses follow from the data alone. Predicted astrometric positions of the tertiary component through five years beyond 2026.5 are provided to guide future high-precision observations.

title: SQUALO II: Probing Accretion Through CO Molecular Outflows in Massive Star-forming Clumps
comment: 24 pages, 13 figures, 3 tables, Accepted for publication in MNRAS
summary: Molecular outflows probe protostellar accretion and mass transfer from clump scales to forming stars. We present an ALMA study of CO (J=2-1) outflows toward 13 massive clumps from the SQUALO sample, spanning a broad evolutionary range and exhibiting clump-scale infall. We identify 51 high-velocity CO lobes associated with 31 outflow systems and derive their physical and dynamical properties assuming local thermodynamic equilibrium. Outflow inferred accretion rates are typically 10^{-5}-10^{-3} Msun/yr, consistent with active massive star formation. The maximum outflow velocity shows little dependence on candidate driving-core mass, indicating that it is not a reliable tracer of protostellar mass in clustered environments. Outflow momentum flux correlates positively with clump surface density, whereas accretion rate shows a tentative, statistically nonsignificant decrease with increasing virial parameter. Total outflow inferred accretion rate shows a tentative positive relation with clump-scale infall rate but remains systematically lower, suggesting that the detected outflows represent only part of the large-scale mass flux. The clump L/M ratio moderately anticorrelates with projected outflow length, although projection, observational limitations, and the embedded source population prevent a unique evolutionary interpretation. Together with the continuum derived fragmentation properties, our results show that compact cores embedded within infalling clumps drive the outflows. The tentative relation between clump-scale infall and protostellar accretion suggests a possible connection across these scales, although our observations do not directly trace mass transfer from filaments to individual protostars.

AI.tldr: An ALMA CO (J=2-1) survey of 13 massive SQUALO clumps identifies 51 high-velocity lobes (31 outflow systems), finding outflow-inferred accretion rates of 10^-5–10^-3 Msun/yr that correlate with clump surface density but only tentatively with clump-scale infall, suggesting compact embedded cores drive outflows while the detected outflows trace only part of the large-scale mass flux.
AI.motivation: Molecular outflows are probes of protostellar accretion and mass transfer across scales (clump to star), yet the link between clump-scale infall and protostellar accretion in massive, clustered star-forming regions remains poorly constrained. The authors aim to characterize outflow properties across a broad evolutionary range of massive clumps exhibiting clump-scale infall and to test which clump/core properties regulate outflow-driven accretion.
AI.method: ALMA CO (J=2-1) observations of 13 massive clumps from the SQUALO sample, spanning a wide evolutionary range and showing clump-scale infall. Identification of high-velocity CO lobes and outflow systems; derivation of physical and dynamical outflow properties (e.g., momentum flux, outflow length, maximum velocity) under local thermodynamic equilibrium (LTE) assumptions; computation of outflow-inferred accretion rates; comparison with candidate driving-core mass, clump surface density, virial parameter, clump-scale infall rate, and clump L/M ratio; combined with continuum-derived fragmentation properties.
AI.result: 51 high-velocity CO lobes in 31 outflow systems. Outflow-inferred accretion rates ~10^-5–10^-3 Msun/yr, consistent with active massive star formation. Maximum outflow velocity shows little dependence on candidate driving-core mass (not a reliable protostellar mass tracer in clustered environments). Outflow momentum flux correlates positively with clump surface density; accretion rate shows a tentative, statistically nonsignificant decrease with virial parameter. Total outflow-inferred accretion rate shows a tentative positive relation with clump-scale infall rate but is systematically lower. Clump L/M ratio moderately anticorrelates with projected outflow length, though projection effects, observational limitations, and embedded source populations preclude a unique evolutionary interpretation.
AI.conclusion: Compact cores embedded within infalling clumps drive the observed outflows. The tentative relation between clump-scale infall and protostellar accretion hints at a possible cross-scale connection, but the observations do not directly trace mass transfer from filaments to individual protostars; detected outflows represent only part of the large-scale mass flux, and projection/observational effects limit evolutionary interpretations.

title: Ensemble Individual Mode Frequency Modeling of Kepler Giants - Extending the IACgrid towards the red-giant branch
comment: Accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics (18 pages, 12 figures)
summary: Precise stellar parameters, in particular ages, are vital for understanding the formation and history of the Milky Way. Usually, this is achieved by fitting stellar evolution models to observational constraints such as spectroscopic and astrometric parameters. Adding global asteroseismic properties to the classical parameters (global seismic modeling) breaks some degeneracies and improves the results. However, this approach has its limitations, with red-giant random age uncertainties usually $\sim$ 20-50%, and often lacking proper quantification of the systematics. We aim to extend seismic modeling to include individual mode frequencies for red-giant branch stars, increasing the number of evolved solar-like oscillators with precise stellar parameters (ages, masses, and radii), and allowing us to quantify the systematics in global seismic modeling. We developed a grid of stellar evolutionary models and computed the individual oscillation frequencies, including a figure of merit to find the best-fitting model. We validate our methodology on a sample of red giants with individual frequency modeling from the literature, finding our masses, radii, and ages in close agreement. We then apply our method to around 100 Kepler red-giant branch stars of near-solar mass and metallicity, which previously have only been modeled with global seismic parameters. We obtain random average uncertainties of 3.4%, 1.3%, and 13.2%, for stellar masses, radii, and ages, respectively. We find that ages from individual mode frequency modeling are significantly, 14% on average, larger than those from global seismic mass-constrained modeling. The modeled luminosities agree within 1.0% with those derived from Gaia parallaxes. We conclude that modeling individual mode frequencies improves age precision by a factor of two for red-giant branch stars, providing stronger constraints for galactic archaeology.

AI.tldr: Modeling individual oscillation mode frequencies for red-giant branch stars yields ages with ~13% random uncertainty, roughly twice as precise as global seismic modeling, and reveals that global seismic ages are systematically ~14% too young.
AI.motivation: Precise stellar ages are essential for reconstructing the formation history of the Milky Way, but standard fitting to spectroscopic and astrometric constraints suffers from degeneracies. Global asteroseismic modeling improves on this but still gives red-giant ages with ~20–50% random uncertainties and poorly quantified systematics.
AI.method: The authors built a grid of stellar evolutionary models and computed individual oscillation mode frequencies, defining a figure of merit to select the best-fitting model. The approach was validated against literature red giants already modeled with individual frequencies, then applied to ~100 near-solar-mass, near-solar-metallicity Kepler red-giant branch stars previously modeled only with global seismic parameters.
AI.result: Validation reproduced literature masses, radii, and ages in close agreement. For the Kepler sample, average random uncertainties are 3.4% (mass), 1.3% (radius), and 13.2% (age). Individual-frequency ages are on average 14% larger than those from global seismic mass-constrained modeling. Modeled luminosities agree within 1.0% of Gaia parallax-derived values.
AI.conclusion: Individual mode frequency modeling doubles the age precision achievable for red-giant branch stars relative to global seismic modeling, quantifies systematics in the latter, and provides stronger constraints for galactic archaeology.
